title: LLM post-training
lead: Turns a base model into an assistant: supervised fine-tuning and its mechanics, low-rank adapters, reward models and RLHF, DPO derived in full, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, together with the evaluation that decides whether any of it worked.
prerequisites: Module 01: expected calibration error; standard errors, the bootstrap and paired comparisons of two models
Module 02: backpropagation, AdamW, learning-rate schedules with warmup, mixed precision
Module 06: the decoder block, causal masking, tied embeddings, parameter counting and the FLOP convention
Module 07: tokenisation and special tokens, sampling and decoding, hallucination, calibration and the abstention scoring rule, the running case study and its workload
Module 08: memory accounting at 16 bytes per trained parameter, activation checkpointing, sequence packing, reserved chat tokens, the case study's continued pretraining
Probability: logistic function, Bernoulli and binomial variables, expectation, KL divergence in nats, standard error of a proportion
Calculus: Lagrange multipliers; the log-derivative identity d log f = df / f
outcomes: By the end you can render a conversation with a chat template, write the masked SFT loss over assistant tokens, and diagnose template, end-of-turn and untrained special-token failures.
By the end you can implement LoRA from scratch, count its trainable parameters, merge it exactly into the base weights, and size LoRA and QLoRA training memory for the 9.5B case-study model.
By the end you can derive the Bradley-Terry model, train a reward model on comparisons, and evaluate it for accuracy against the label-noise ceiling, calibration and overoptimisation.
By the end you can derive the policy gradient with a baseline and explain PPO's clipped objective and why RLHF with PPO holds four models in memory.
By the end you can derive the closed-form optimum of the KL-regularised objective and the DPO loss from it, implement DPO, and recognise likelihood displacement from off-policy pairs.
By the end you can implement GRPO with group-relative advantages and a KL term, predict which groups carry no signal, and design a verifiable reward that a degenerate output cannot satisfy.
By the end you can build a behavioural evaluation suite with programmatic checkers and report pass rates with bootstrap confidence intervals, paired differences and an exact test.
By the end you can explain how refusals, abstention, honesty and tool use are trained, and how over-refusal, sycophancy and guessing arise from the training signal.
By the end you can plan a post-training recipe for a domain model with explicit data, compute arithmetic and promotion gates, and justify each choice.
software: PyTorch 2.x (CPU is enough; Google Colab is the free GPU option)
Download: HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M, about 270 MB (Labs 1 and 2, and the base model in Lab 6)

sections.title: What post-training is for
sections.purpose: Say what a base model lacks, what post-training installs, why it is cheap and fragile, and the order in which its three families are usually applied.
must_cover: A base model (Module 08) is a model of text: it completes 'The three ISO 26262 ASIL parameters are' correctly and continues 'Q: What are they? A:' with something, but has no notion of being asked, no preferred format, no sense of when to stop, no refusals and no tools.

Post-training installs behaviour on top of knowledge, with thousands to millions of examples against trillions of pretraining tokens: that is why it is cheap, why one organisation with one GPU can do it, and why it can go wrong quickly (a small signal steers the model).

Evidence that behaviour is cheap relative to capability: labellers preferred the outputs of InstructGPT's 1.3B model to those of the 175B GPT-3, a model 100 times larger (Ouyang et al. 2022); LIMA reached strong assistant behaviour from 1,000 curated examples on a 65B base (Zhou et al. 2023), the 'superficial alignment' view, stated and then qualified (it holds for format and style, not for skills the base lacks).

The three families in their usual order: SFT (demonstrations), preference optimisation (pairs), reinforcement learning (generate, score, push probability toward high scores); with a verifiable reward RL is the most powerful of the three. Parameter-efficient methods (Section 4) apply to all of them.

A table with one row per stage: data unit, training signal, what it teaches, typical scale, what dominates cost (SFT: conversations, token log-likelihood, format and task framing, 10^3-10^6 examples, tokens; preferences: (prompt, chosen, rejected), pairwise likelihood, comparative judgements, 10^4-10^6 pairs, labelling; RL: prompts plus a reward, sampled returns, behaviour that must generalise, 10^3-10^5 prompts, generation).

Four published pipelines as patterns, not recipes: InstructGPT (SFT, reward model, PPO); Llama 2-Chat (SFT, then iterated rounds of rejection sampling and PPO); Tulu 3 (SFT, DPO, then RL with verifiable rewards, the paper that named RLVR); DeepSeek-R1 (cold-start SFT, reasoning RL, rejection-sampling SFT, RL for all scenarios).

The running case study introduced in Module 07, restated as a hypothetical: an open-weight bilingual (English-Chinese) ~9.5B model with base and instruct releases, adapted to draft and check safety-case arguments for the pressure-relief system of a reactor vessel. Module 08 chose continued pretraining (CPT) on 2B tokens of safety-engineering text for it, so this module's SFT starts from the CPT checkpoint (Section 14 gives the rule for choosing the starting point). What post-training must add: chat behaviour, which a continued-pretrained base lacks; the argument format and its structural rules; honesty about missing evidence; edit discipline. What it cannot add: domain knowledge the base lacks, which is what the continued pretraining was for.
worked_examples: Scale ratio: the case study's ~50M SFT tokens against Module 08's pretraining figures: 50e6 / 2e12 = 2.5e-5 (0.0025%) of the 2T tokens of its illustrative pretraining plan for a base of this size, and 50e6 / 15e12 = 3.3e-6 of the 15T tokens on which the strongest open models of this size were trained as of 2026; even against the team's own 2B-token continued pretraining it is 2.5%.

Base versus instruct, real outputs from Lab 6 (SmolLM2-135M, same ChatML prompt, greedy): asked 'How many millimetres are in 2.5 metres? Reply with the number only.', the base model repeats the question and trails commas; the instruct model answers in assistant form, '2.5 meters is approximately 5.56 inches.', and is wrong. Post-training installed the turn-taking and the stopping, not the arithmetic or the instruction-following.

checks: Why can post-training run on one GPU when pretraining needs thousands? -> Its signal is 10^4 to 10^6 times smaller in tokens (the case study: 50M against 2T, one forty-thousandth); the knowledge is already in the weights and only behaviour is being changed.

A base model answers 'Q: What are the three ASIL parameters? A:' correctly. Why is it still not an assistant? -> It has no notion of a turn ending, a format, a refusal or a tool; another 'Q:' is as likely a continuation as a stop.

sections.title: Supervised fine-tuning: the data
sections.purpose: Define an SFT example, list where good ones come from, and show why quality, coverage and distribution match beat volume.
must_cover: An SFT example is a conversation: a system prompt, one or more user turns, and the assistant turns the model should have produced; multi-turn conversations; tool turns (forward pointer to Section 11). Stored as a list of {role, content} messages with a manifest entry recording source and licence.

Human-written demonstrations: highest quality and most expensive. LIMA: 1,000 excellent examples outperform much larger mediocre sets; SFT teaches how to behave, and the model already knows most of what it needs.

Distillation: a stronger model answers the prompts, its answers are the targets, filtered by a checker or judge. Most open instruction datasets are built this way. Check that the teacher's licence and terms permit it.
Self-generation with filtering: the model's own samples, kept when they pass a verifier (Section 8). The cheapest source when a verifier exists.
Synthetic edits: for behaviours such as 'change only what was asked', apply scripted modifications to real artifacts so that the target is exact.

Quality filters and coverage: exact and near-duplicate removal, length and language checks, verifier pass, judge-score thresholds; task diversity matters more than count; decontaminate against every evaluation set (Section 12).

Distribution match: the same system prompts, the same chat template, the same languages in the same proportions, prompts as messy as real ones. A model trained on tidy English briefs and served Chinese ones with typos has been trained on the wrong distribution.

Selection bias from filtering: keeping only verified answers removes the prompts the teacher cannot solve, so the student never sees the hardest cases; cap examples per prompt so easy prompts do not dominate.

Mixing general instruction data into a narrow set to limit forgetting; the share is tuned by watching a general evaluation, not fixed by rule (the case study's choice and its reasoning are in Section 14).
worked_examples: Distillation yield: 20,000 prompts, one teacher sample each, checker pass rate 62% -> 12,400 kept. Sampling 4 per prompt and keeping the best passing one covers 1 - 0.38^4 = 97.9% of prompts if failures were independent; in practice the uncovered 2-10% are the hard prompts, which is exactly the selection bias.

sections.title: Supervised fine-tuning: templates, masking, packing and limits
sections.purpose: Show how a conversation becomes a training sequence and a loss, which hyperparameters matter, and what SFT can and cannot change in a model.
must_cover:
The chat template renders messages into tokens with special markers per role; ChatML as the running example: '<|im_start|>role
' + content + '<|im_end|>
', and the generation prompt '<|im_start|>assistant
'. The template used in training must be byte-identical to the one used at serving; a default system prompt inserted by one side only (the SmolLM2-Instruct template inserts 'You are a helpful AI assistant named SmolLM, trained by Hugging Face' when none is given) or a missing newline is enough to change the tokens.

Untrained template tokens: a base tokenizer can reserve chat tokens that pretraining never used (Module 08). In SmolLM2-135M the embedding rows of <|im_start|> and <|im_end|> have cosine similarity 0.9998 and sit in a cluster with other never-trained tokens; with tied embeddings the model cannot tell 'end of turn' from them. Fix: before training, initialise those rows by sampling from a Gaussian fitted to the trained rows (per-dimension mean and standard deviation, a diagonal version of Hewitt's 2021 suggestion), which makes them distinct and typical; Labs 1 and 2 do this and show what happens without it. The case study's continued-pretrained base may not have trained its chat tokens either; Section 14 checks them with Lab 1's cosine test and initialises them.

The SFT objective written out: L(theta) = -(1 / sum_t m_t) sum_t m_t log p_theta(x_t | x_<t), with m_t = 1 on assistant tokens including the end-of-turn token and 0 elsewhere; show it equals the negative conditional log-likelihood of the response given the prompt because log p(y|x) = sum over response positions of log p(y_t | x, y_<t). Labels are the inputs shifted by one position; masked positions get label -100 in PyTorch's cross-entropy.

Why mask: the model is not being taught to predict users or system prompts; the gradient budget goes to the response; the end-of-turn token must be in the loss because predicting it is how the model learns to stop.

Loss normalisation: the mean over all trained tokens in a batch weights long replies more than a per-sequence mean; with gradient accumulation the summed loss must be divided by the total number of trained tokens across all micro-batches, not averaged per micro-batch.

Packing: several short conversations concatenated into one training row, with a block-diagonal attention mask and position ids restarting per conversation so that they cannot see each other; the arithmetic of padding waste.

Hyperparameters: full fine-tuning at a learning rate of 1-2e-5, LoRA at 1-2e-4; cosine schedule with a short warmup (about 3% of steps); 1-3 epochs; a batch of 16-128 sequences; sequence length covering the longest real example; weight decay small or zero.

Evaluation during SFT: held-out loss and the task metrics that matter (for the case study, the fraction of replies that parse and the fraction that pass the structural checker) after every epoch; the loss can fall while the task metric does not, and the reverse.

What SFT can and cannot do: it reliably teaches format, style, task framing, the shape of a refusal and which of the model's abilities to deploy; it does not reliably add knowledge: a fact seen a few times is learned brittlely, and fine-tuning on facts the base does not know raises hallucination (Gekhman et al. 2024: such examples are fitted late, and fitting them increases hallucination). Knowledge belongs in pretraining or continued pretraining (Module 08); behaviour belongs here.

Forgetting: a narrow SFT set degrades general ability; measured by keeping a general evaluation in the loop; mitigated by mixing general instruction data and by training adapters rather than all weights.

Teacher forcing (Module 04): SFT trains on perfect prefixes; at generation the model conditions on its own outputs and errors compound. This is one reason later stages train on the model's own samples (Sections 6-9).
worked_examples: Real token accounting with the SmolLM2 tokenizer: system 'You are a concise engineering assistant.', user 'Convert 2.5 MPa to kPa.', assistant '2500 kPa' renders to 40 tokens. The assistant header '<|im_start|>assistant\n' is 4 tokens (masked); the target is 7 tokens: '2', '5', '0', '0', ' k', 'Pa', '<|im_end|>' (digits are single tokens). 7 of 40 tokens (17.5%) carry loss; across Lab 1's training set the figure is 9%.

Normalisation trap: micro-batch A has 10 trained tokens with summed loss 20.0, micro-batch B has 90 with summed loss 90.0. The correct token mean is 110 / 100 = 1.10; averaging the two micro-batch means gives (2.0 + 1.0) / 2 = 1.50.

Packing: 1,000 conversations of mean length 300 tokens and maximum 2,048. Padding each to 2,048 processes 2.048M token slots for 0.30M real tokens (85% waste). Packing into 2,048-token rows needs ceil(300,000 / 2,048) = 147 rows: 6.8 times fewer slots.
Schedule: 9,600 conversations, batch 64, 3 epochs -> 150 steps per epoch, 450 steps in all, warmup 14 steps (3%).

Lab 1's evidence (SmolLM2-135M, 240 synthetic conversations, 15 steps of full fine-tuning): stop rate 0% -> 100%, exact match 0% -> 74%; unit conversion and value extraction 100%, two-digit sums 80% (the base, given three worked examples in a plain completion prompt, already gets 38% right), the PASS/FAIL limit check 40% (the base's three-shot score is 58% against a 52% share of PASS answers, i.e. near chance): format arrives in a few steps, a comparison the base cannot do barely moves.

Annotations: 'header masked', 'end-of-turn token trained: this is how the model learns to stop', and a callout 'training and serving must render these bytes identically'.

Packing versus padding. Top: three conversations of 700, 900 and 400 tokens each padded to 2,048 in separate rows, padding greyed (3 x 2,048 slots for 2,000 tokens). Bottom: the same three packed into one 2,048-token row, with the attention mask drawn as a 2,048 x 2,048 matrix containing three lower-triangular blocks on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere, and position ids restarting at 0 at each boundary.

checks: Why must <|im_end|> be in the loss? -> Predicting it is how the model learns to stop; mask it and the model never ends its turn.

Training loss falls steadily but the checker pass rate is flat. Name two causes. -> The loss is dominated by easy tokens (format, boilerplate) while the few tokens that decide correctness barely improve; or the training targets and the evaluation parser disagree on format (a template or parse mismatch).

Lab 1's model writes the right answer and then a junk token instead of <|im_end|>. What happened? -> The end-of-turn row was never trained and is nearly identical to other untrained rows; initialise it from the trained rows' statistics, or train longer.

sections.title: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning: LoRA and QLoRA
sections.purpose: Derive LoRA, size it for the case-study model, and show how QLoRA puts fine-tuning of the 9.5B model on a 24 GB GPU.
must_cover: The memory problem: full fine-tuning at 16 bytes per parameter (bf16 weights 2, bf16 gradients 2, fp32 master weights 4, Adam moments 4 + 4; Module 08) is 9.55e9 x 16 = 152.8 GB of model states for the case-study model; the optimiser state is most of it. Units, stated once: memory in this module is in decimal GB (10^9 bytes), as in Modules 07, 08 and 10; GPU capacities are their marketed sizes (24, 48, 80 GB), which are binary (a 24 GB card holds about 24 GiB, 25.8 GB), so comparisons against them leave a little headroom.

LoRA (Hu et al. 2022): freeze W in R^{d x k} and learn W' = W + (alpha / r) B A with B in R^{d x r}, A in R^{r x k}, r << min(d, k). The forward pass is h = W x + (alpha / r) B (A x); B A is never formed during training. rank(B A) <= r. Motivation: fine-tuning updates have low intrinsic dimension (Aghajanyan et al. 2021).

Initialisation derived: A random (Gaussian or Kaiming), B = 0, so W' = W at step 0 and training starts from the base exactly. With g = dL/dh: dL/dB = (alpha / r) g (A x)^T is non-zero and dL/dA = (alpha / r) B^T g x^T is zero at step 0, so B moves first; if both were zero, both gradients would vanish for ever.

The alpha / r scaling keeps the size of the update roughly constant as r changes, so the learning rate need not be retuned for each rank; alpha = r or alpha = 2r are common choices; one sentence on rank-stabilised LoRA (alpha / sqrt(r), Kalajdzievski 2023).

Parameter count r (d + k) per matrix; which layers: all linear layers of every block (q, k, v, o, gate, up, down). Attention-only adapters underfit; the QLoRA paper found adapters on all linear layers were needed to match full fine-tuning.
Embeddings and head usually stay frozen; never-trained special tokens then need their rows initialised or made trainable (Section 3, Lab 2).

Memory: base in bf16 (2 bytes per parameter) plus the adapter's training state at 16 bytes per adapter parameter plus activations: with full checkpointing 3.61 GB for one 8,192-token sequence by Module 08's formula (12d + 4 n_kv d_head + 6 d_ff = 145,408 bytes per token per layer): 2.42 GB of stored layer inputs (67 MB per layer) plus 1.19 GB for the layer being recomputed. The fp32 logits, 8,192 x 152,064 x 4 B = 4.98 GB, are avoided by computing the loss in chunks (Module 08).

Compute, under Module 06's FLOP convention, recalled once here with a link: a forward pass costs 2 N_matmul FLOPs per token, with N_matmul = N - V d = 8.93e9 for the case study because the input-embedding lookup does no arithmetic, plus attention, 4Ldt at context t, which averages 2LdT over a causal sequence of length T; training costs three times the forward pass, 6 N_matmul + 6LTd = 6.08e10 FLOPs per token at T = 8,192 (attention adds 13.5%). LoRA saves memory, not much arithmetic: the forward pass and the activation-gradient half of the backward still run through every frozen weight, and attention, which has no weights, keeps its whole backward; only the matmuls' weight-gradient half (2 N_matmul) disappears: 4 N_matmul + 6LTd = 4.30e10 FLOPs per token, 29% less. The LoRA paper reports 10,000 times fewer trainable parameters and 3 times less GPU memory than Adam fine-tuning of GPT-3 175B. GPU-hours here use an assumed sustained 4e14 FLOP/s per H100 (40% of the 989 TFLOP/s dense bf16 peak; Module 08), labelled as an assumption wherever it is used.

Merging: W <- W + (alpha / r) B A, one addition per matrix, after which the adapter costs nothing at inference; or keep adapters separate so several share one base in memory and are swapped per request (multi-adapter serving, Module 10). Merging into a quantised base needs dequantise-add-requantise, which changes the result: merge into bf16 weights, then quantise for serving and evaluate again.

QLoRA (Dettmers et al. 2023): the frozen base stored in 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4): 16 levels at quantiles of a standard normal rescaled to [-1, 1] with an exact zero; weights quantised in blocks of 64 with one absmax scale per block; double quantisation stores the scales in 8 bits (overhead 0.5 -> 0.127 bits per parameter); weights are dequantised to bf16 on the fly for each matrix multiply; the adapter trains in bf16/fp32; paged optimisers move optimiser state to CPU memory during spikes. The paper fine-tunes a 65B model on one 48 GB GPU. Quantisation in depth is Module 10's.

When to fine-tune everything: with tens of millions of tokens or more, or a task far from the base's distribution, full fine-tuning gains a few points; below that, LoRA matches it. LoRA also forgets less (Biderman et al. 2024, 'LoRA learns less and forgets less'). Continued pretraining is done on full weights; SFT and preference stages usually on adapters.
worked_examples: One 4096 x 4096 matrix at r = 64: 2 x 64 x 4096 = 524,288 adapter parameters against 16,777,216 (3.1%).

The case-study model (Module 07's configuration, used unchanged in Modules 07-10: 36 layers, d = 4,096, 32 query heads and 8 KV heads of dimension 128, SwiGLU width 15,360, vocabulary 152,064, untied embeddings: 9,550,729,216 parameters, of which 8,305,016,832 in the blocks and 622,854,144 in each of the embedding and the output head). Per layer the seven projections give r x 84,992 adapter parameters (q 8,192r, k 5,120r, v 5,120r, o 8,192r, gate, up and down 19,456r each). r = 64: 195,821,568 (2.05%), training state 3.13 GB, against 152.8 GB of model states for full fine-tuning. (Exercise e4 asks for r = 16; do not work it here.)
LoRA memory at r = 64 for one 8,192-token sequence: 19.10 GB bf16 base + 3.13 GB adapter state + 3.61 GB of checkpointed activations = 25.8 GB, comfortable on one 80 GB GPU and possible on 40-48 GB.

SmolLM2-135M (Lab 2): r = 8 on all seven projections in 30 layers: 30 x 81,408 = 2,442,240 trainable parameters, 1.78% of the 136,957,248 total; Adam state 19.5 MB against 1,076 MB for full fine-tuning.

NF4 on one block of eight weights (0.031, -0.012, 0.004, -0.027, 0.018, 0.0, -0.006, 0.022): absmax 0.031; normalised (1.0, -0.387, 0.129, -0.871, 0.581, 0.0, -0.194, 0.710); nearest NF4 levels (1.0, -0.395, 0.161, -1.0, 0.563, 0.0, -0.185, 0.723); dequantised (0.031, -0.0122, 0.0050, -0.031, 0.0174, 0.0, -0.0057, 0.0224). The -0.027 weight falls in NF4's widest gap (between -0.696 and -1.0) and on this block uniform int4 does better; the advantage is statistical: over 6.4M normally distributed weights in blocks of 64, NF4's relative squared error is 0.85% against 1.16% for uniform int4.

QLoRA memory for the case-study model: block linear weights 8.305e9 x 4.127 bits = 4.28 GB; embedding and output head kept in bf16, 1.246e9 x 2 B = 2.49 GB; base 6.78 GB; plus the r = 64 adapter's 3.13 GB and 3.61 GB of checkpointed activations: 13.5 GB, which fits a 24 GB GPU.

FLOPs: LoRA SFT on 50M tokens for 2 epochs is 1e8 token-passes over packed 8,192-token rows (the attention term at T = 8,192 is an upper bound when the packing mask is block-diagonal): 4.30e10 x 1e8 = 4.30e18 FLOPs, 3.0 GPU-hours at the assumed 4e14 FLOP/s; full fine-tuning: 6.08e18 FLOPs, 4.2 GPU-hours, and its 152.8 GB of model states do not fit one GPU.

checks: Why B = 0 and not A = 0? -> Either makes the update zero at the start; with B = 0 and A random, B receives a non-zero gradient at once; with both zero, neither ever does.

LoRA cut the trainable parameters fifty-fold. Why did the step time fall much less? -> The forward pass and the activation gradients still run through every frozen weight, and attention keeps its whole backward; only the matmuls' weight gradients are saved: about 4 N_matmul rather than 6 N_matmul FLOPs per token.

sections.title: Preferences and reward models
sections.purpose: Explain why comparisons are collected, derive the Bradley-Terry model that turns them into a scalar reward, and show how a reward model is trained, checked and over-optimised.
must_cover: A demonstration says what is right; a preference says which of two outputs is better. Pairs are easier to collect than demonstrations, capture what is hard to demonstrate (tone, safety, helpfulness), and are the raw material of RLHF and DPO.

Collecting preferences: sample two or more responses per prompt from the current model (on-policy), labellers or a judge choose; rankings of K responses give K(K-1)/2 pairs (InstructGPT ranked 4 to 9 responses per prompt and trained on all pairs from one prompt as a single batch element, because treating correlated pairs as independent overfitted); ties.
Agreement sets a ceiling: InstructGPT reports that its labellers agreed with each other about 73% of the time; no reward model can be meaningfully more accurate than its labels.

Bradley-Terry derived as a random-utility model: perceived quality u = r(x, y) + epsilon with epsilon independent standard Gumbel; the difference of two standard Gumbels is standard logistic, so p(y_w > y_l | x) = sigma(r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l)). The log-odds of a preference are linear in the reward difference. Elo is the same model in base 10 with scale 400.

Shift invariance: adding c(x) to every reward for prompt x changes no probability, so rewards are identified only up to a per-prompt constant; normalise them (subtract a per-prompt or global baseline) before using them in RL.

The reward model: a copy of the language model (initialised from the SFT model) with the unembedding replaced by a scalar head read at the final token; trained to maximise the BT likelihood: L_RM = -E[log sigma(r_phi(x, y_w) - r_phi(x, y_l))]. Its gradient is -(1 - sigma(Delta)) (grad r_w - grad r_l): pairs it already ranks confidently contribute little.

Evaluating a reward model: held-out pairwise accuracy compared with the label-noise ceiling; calibration (reliability diagram and expected calibration error, recalled in one line with a link to Module 01, Section 7, at this first use in the module); behaviour away from the training distribution, where a learned reward is least trustworthy.

Overoptimisation (Goodhart's law): optimising a learned proxy raises the proxy and, past a point, lowers the true reward (Gao et al. 2023). Best-of-n against a reward model is the simplest optimiser and already shows it (Lab 3; Section 8 for best-of-n as a policy).
Biases learned rewards inherit from labellers and judges: longer answers preferred, agreement with the user preferred (sycophancy, Section 10), list formatting preferred.

One paragraph on outcome versus process reward models: an outcome model scores the final answer; a process model scores each step (Lightman et al. 2023); DeepSeek-R1 reported that a process reward model was hacked at scale and used rule-based outcome rewards instead.
worked_examples: BT numbers: r_w = 1.2, r_l = 0.3, Delta = 0.9 -> p = sigma(0.9) = 0.711, loss -ln 0.711 = 0.341, gradient magnitude with respect to Delta 1 - 0.711 = 0.289. Reversed (Delta = -0.9): loss 1.241, gradient magnitude 0.711: wrongly ranked pairs drive learning.
Elo: a 200-point gap gives 1 / (1 + 10^(-0.5)) = 0.760, the same as a reward difference of 200 ln 10 / 400 = 1.151 nats.

Lab 3 (synthetic two-feature responses, true reward r*(x) = 2 x1 + x2 - 0.5 |x|^2, 4,000 BT-labelled training pairs): an MLP reward model reaches 0.836 held-out accuracy against 0.852 for the true reward itself (the ceiling set by label noise), expected calibration error 0.024, correlation 0.967 with r*, and a mean reward of -8.0 on the data, an arbitrary offset that shift invariance permits.

Overoptimisation in Lab 3: best-of-n selection against a linear reward model raises the true reward of the pick from -0.95 (n = 1) to 1.92 at n = 64, then lowers it to 0.37 at n = 16,384 while the proxy keeps rising from 1.0 to 6.1; selecting with the true reward climbs to 2.50.

Marked points: Delta = 0.9 (p 0.711, loss 0.341) and Delta = -0.9 (p 0.289, loss 1.241); a shaded band labelled 'labeller agreement ~73%' indicating the accuracy ceiling.

Curves: proxy reward of the linear RM's pick (rising), true reward of the linear RM's pick (rises to 1.92 then falls to 0.37), true reward of the MLP RM's pick (rises to 1.87 then declines gently to 1.63), true reward of the oracle pick (rising to 2.50).

A reward model reaches 70% held-out accuracy; the labellers agree 73% of the time. Is it badly underfitting? -> Probably not much: label noise caps achievable accuracy near the agreement rate.

sections.title: RLHF with PPO
sections.purpose: State the KL-regularised RL objective, derive the policy gradient it needs, and explain how PPO optimises it with four models in memory.
must_cover: RLHF as InstructGPT did it: SFT; a reward model on comparisons of the SFT model's outputs; then reinforcement learning of the policy pi_theta against the reward with a penalty for drifting from the SFT model: max_theta E_{x ~ D, y ~ pi_theta(.|x)}[ r_phi(x, y) - beta log(pi_theta(y|x) / pi_ref(y|x)) ], whose expectation is E[r_phi] - beta KL(pi_theta || pi_ref).

The KL term is not decoration: the reward model is accurate only near the distribution it was trained on; without the penalty the policy finds outputs it scores highly for reasons unrelated to quality (reward hacking) and collapses onto a few responses. Section 7 shows the objective has a closed-form optimum.

The policy gradient derived: grad_theta E_{y ~ pi_theta}[R(y)] = sum_y R(y) grad pi_theta(y) = E[R(y) grad log pi_theta(y)] (log-derivative trick); for a sequence, grad log pi(y|x) = sum_t grad log pi(y_t | x, y_<t). A baseline b leaves the gradient unbiased because E[grad log pi] = sum_y grad pi(y) = grad 1 = 0, and reduces its variance; A = R - b is the advantage.
RLHF as a token-level problem: state = prompt plus tokens so far, action = next token, reward = -beta log(pi_theta / pi_ref) at every token plus r_phi(x, y) at the last.

PPO (Schulman et al. 2017): reuse each batch of samples for several gradient steps with the importance ratio rho_t = pi_theta(y_t | .) / pi_old(y_t | .), and maximise the clipped surrogate min(rho_t A_t, clip(rho_t, 1 - epsilon, 1 + epsilon) A_t), epsilon = 0.2: a pessimistic bound that removes the incentive to move the ratio beyond 1 +/- epsilon in a helpful direction while always penalising harmful moves.
A learned value function V(s) as a per-token baseline; generalised advantage estimation at concept level (lambda trades bias against variance); the value loss.

Four models: policy (trained), value (trained), reference (frozen), reward (frozen); a generation loop in the middle of training; a long list of implementation details (reward normalisation, advantage whitening, KL control, value clipping) that decide whether it works.
InstructGPT's 'alignment tax' (regressions on public NLP benchmarks after RLHF) and PPO-ptx, which mixes pretraining-gradient updates into PPO to reduce it.
PPO produced the first assistants; its cost and fragility are why DPO exists.
worked_examples: Policy gradient on a three-response bandit: pi = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2) from softmax logits, R = (0, 1, 2). E[R] = 0.7; the exact gradient with respect to the logits is pi_k (R_k - E[R]) = (-0.35, 0.09, 0.26). One sample y = 3 with baseline 0.7 gives A = 1.3 and the estimate (e_3 - pi) A = (-0.65, -0.39, 1.04); averaged over samples the estimate equals the exact gradient. Its mean squared norm is 1.018 without a baseline and 0.445 with b = E[R]: the variance falls from 0.820 to 0.247.

PPO clipping, epsilon = 0.2: (rho = 1.3, A = +1.5) -> min(1.95, 1.80) = 1.80, clipped, no gradient; (rho = 0.7, A = -1.5) -> min(-1.05, -1.20) = -1.20, clipped; (rho = 1.3, A = -1.5) -> min(-1.95, -1.80) = -1.95, unclipped, the harmful move is penalised in full; (rho = 0.7, A = +1.5) -> 1.05, unclipped.
Sequence reward: the reward model gives 2.0; the 50-token response's summed log-ratio log(pi_theta / pi_ref) is 5.0 nats; with beta = 0.05 the total reward is 2.0 - 0.25 = 1.75.

Memory for PPO with full fine-tuning of the 9.55B case-study model: policy 152.8 GB (16 B per parameter) + value 142.9 GB (the same network with a scalar head in place of the 0.62B-parameter output head: 8.93e9 parameters) + reference 19.1 GB (frozen, bf16) + reward 17.9 GB (frozen, bf16, scalar head) = 332.6 GB before activations and the generation cache. With LoRA: one 19.1 GB bf16 base shared by the policy, the reference (adapter switched off) and the value trunk (a second adapter and a scalar head), two adapters at 3.13 GB each, and the reward model's own 17.9 GB: 43.2 GB.

The four models are boxes: policy (orange border, 'trained, 152.8 GB'), value (orange, 'trained, 142.9 GB, scalar head'), reference (grey, 'frozen, 19.1 GB') and reward (grey, 'frozen, 17.9 GB, scalar head'), with the totals noted beneath: 332.6 GB with full fine-tuning, 43.2 GB with LoRA (one shared base).

Right, A < 0: flat below 1 - epsilon, then falling linearly as rho increases, never flat on the harmful side. The four worked points marked.

checks: Why subtract a baseline? -> It leaves the expected gradient unchanged, because E[grad log pi] = 0, and reduces its variance (0.820 to 0.247 in the bandit example).
Why is (rho = 1.3, A = -1.5) not clipped? -> The min picks the more pessimistic term; moves that hurt are always penalised in full; only helpful moves beyond 1 +/- epsilon are cut off.

sections.title: Direct preference optimisation
sections.purpose: Derive DPO in full from the KL-regularised objective, explain what beta does, and show how DPO fails and what its variants change.
must_cover: Step 1, the closed-form optimum. For a fixed prompt, maximise sum_y pi(y) [ r(y) - beta log(pi(y) / pi_ref(y)) ] subject to sum_y pi(y) = 1. Derivation (a): rewrite as -beta KL(pi || pi_ref e^{r/beta} / Z) + beta log Z with Z(x) = sum_y pi_ref(y|x) e^{r(x,y)/beta}; the KL is minimised (zero) at pi* = pi_ref e^{r/beta} / Z (Gibbs' inequality). Derivation (b): the Lagrangian condition r(y) - beta (log(pi(y) / pi_ref(y)) + 1) - lambda = 0 gives the same result. The optimal value of the objective is beta log Z(x).
Step 2, invert: r(x, y) = beta log(pi*(y|x) / pi_ref(y|x)) + beta log Z(x).

Step 3, substitute into Bradley-Terry: the beta log Z(x) terms cancel in the difference for two responses to the same prompt, leaving p(y_w > y_l | x) = sigma(beta log(pi*(y_w|x) / pi_ref(y_w|x)) - beta log(pi*(y_l|x) / pi_ref(y_l|x))).

Step 4, fit the policy to the preference data directly, with no reward model and no sampling (Rafailov et al. 2023): L_DPO(theta) = -E[ log sigma( beta log(pi_theta(y_w|x) / pi_ref(y_w|x)) - beta log(pi_theta(y_l|x) / pi_ref(y_l|x)) ) ].

The reparameterisation loses no generality (every reward equivalence class under shift contains a reward of this form; the paper's Theorem 1), and beta log(pi_theta / pi_ref) is the implicit reward: 'your language model is secretly a reward model'.

The gradient written out: grad L = -beta E[ sigma(-u) (grad log pi_theta(y_w|x) - grad log pi_theta(y_l|x)) ], u the margin; it raises the likelihood of y_w and lowers that of y_l, weighted by how wrong the implicit reward currently is: hard pairs get large updates, already-correct pairs small ones.
The source's dpo_loss code, with the arguments defined as sums of assistant-token log-probabilities under the policy and the frozen reference (the masking of Section 3).

Practice: two forward passes per sequence (policy and reference; reference log-probabilities can be computed once in advance; with LoRA the reference is the base with the adapter switched off), an ordinary supervised loop, results comparable to PPO on preference data in the DPO paper. beta around 0.1; learning rate 5e-7 to 5e-6 for full weights; one to two epochs.

What beta means: the temperature of pi*: small beta lets the policy move far from the reference (large KL) and exploit any error in the reward; large beta keeps it close. In DPO, beta also sets the margin at which the loss saturates. The widget makes this visible.

What goes wrong (1): DPO works best on pairs sampled from a policy close to the one being trained; on pairs from a distant model it can lower the likelihood of both responses while widening their gap (likelihood displacement; Razin et al. 2024), and the mass removed goes to responses in neither column. Lab 4 reproduces it.

What goes wrong (2): with deterministic preferences (y_w always wins) the optimum sends pi(y_l) to zero whatever beta is (the IPO paper's argument), so early stopping and held-out evaluation matter. (3) It prefers longer responses unless the data is length-controlled (Park et al. 2024). (4) It is only as good as the pairs. Remedy for (1): on-policy or iterative DPO, regenerating pairs from the current policy each round.

Variants, one loss line each: IPO replaces the log-sigmoid with a squared loss toward a fixed margin, (h - 1/(2 tau))^2 with h the log-ratio difference; KTO uses single outputs labelled good or bad, without pairs; ORPO adds an odds-ratio preference term to the SFT loss with no reference model; SimPO uses the length-normalised log-probability (beta / |y|) log pi_theta(y|x) as the reward with a target margin gamma and no reference. None dominates; DPO remains the default.
DPO versus PPO: careful comparisons find that well-tuned PPO can outperform DPO (Xu et al. 2024); the usual explanation is that PPO trains on its own samples.
worked_examples: Three responses, pi_ref = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2), r = (0, 1, 2). beta = 1: weights 0.5, 0.3e, 0.2e^2 = 0.500, 0.815, 1.478; Z = 2.793; pi* = (0.179, 0.292, 0.529); KL(pi* || pi_ref) = 0.323 nats; E[r] = 1.350 against 0.700 under pi_ref; objective 1.350 - 0.323 = 1.027 = ln 2.793 = beta log Z. Implicit rewards beta log(pi*/pi_ref) = (-1.027, -0.027, 0.973) = r - beta log Z. beta = 0.5: pi* = (0.037, 0.163, 0.801), KL 0.916, E[r] 1.764. As beta -> 0 the policy collapses on y_3 and the KL tends to -ln 0.2 = 1.609: collapsing onto a rare response costs -log of its reference probability.

DPO loss by hand, beta = 0.1: at initialisation (policy = reference) the margin is 0 and the loss is ln 2 = 0.693 for every pair. Policy log-probabilities (chosen -12.0, rejected -14.0), reference (-12.5, -13.0): implicit rewards +0.05 and -0.10, margin 0.15, loss 0.621, gradient weight sigma(-0.15) = 0.463. Displacement case: policy (-13.0, -17.0) against the same reference: margin 0.35, loss 0.533, lower than before, while the chosen response became less likely than under the reference (implicit reward -0.05).

Lab 4's exact check on an 8-response bandit (pi_ref = (0.30, 0.20, 0.15, 0.12, 0.10, 0.06, 0.04, 0.03), r = (0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 0.2, -0.5, 1.5, 0.8, 2.0), 20,000 BT-labelled pairs): DPO lands within 0.04 of pi* everywhere; KL(pi_DPO || pi_ref) = 2.23, 0.80, 0.19, 0.045 for beta = 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2 against the closed-form 2.38, 0.90, 0.215, 0.049.

Lab 4 on the toy sums policy (beta = 0.1, 300 steps): on-policy pairs raise sampled accuracy from 0.45 to 0.92 with KL 0.80 and chosen log-ratio +0.70; off-policy pairs (rejected responses are random digit strings) reach pair accuracy 1.00 and loss 0.014 while accuracy falls to 0.37, the chosen log-ratio goes to -0.50 and the KL to 1.85.

figures.description: The DPO derivation as a chain of five boxes joined by labelled arrows: (1) KL-regularised objective -> [Gibbs' inequality or Lagrangian] -> (2) pi* = pi_ref exp(r / beta) / Z(x) -> [take logs, solve for r] -> (3) r = beta log(pi*/pi_ref) + beta log Z(x) -> [substitute into Bradley-Terry; same prompt, Z cancels] -> (4) p(y_w > y_l) in terms of policies only -> [replace pi* by pi_theta, maximise likelihood] -> (5) L_DPO. Z(x) is struck through in box 4.

Lab 4's DPO training curves, on-policy (solid) versus off-policy pairs (dashed), three panels sharing an x-axis of training steps 0-300: (a) DPO loss (off-policy near zero quickly); (b) mean chosen and rejected log-ratios log(pi_theta / pi_ref) (chosen rises to +0.70 on-policy, falls to -0.50 off-policy; rejected falls in both); (c) sampled task accuracy (0.45 -> 0.92 on-policy; 0.45 -> 0.37 off-policy).

checks: Why does Z(x) never need to be computed in DPO? -> It depends only on the prompt and cancels in the difference of implicit rewards for two responses to the same prompt.
Raising beta from 0.1 to 0.5 with the same data: does the policy move more or less? -> Less: pi* = pi_ref e^{r/beta} / Z is flatter, and the DPO loss saturates at a smaller log-ratio margin.
What is the DPO loss when the policy equals the reference? -> ln 2 = 0.693 for every pair.

sections.title: The simplest reinforcement learning: sample, verify, keep
sections.purpose: Introduce verifiable rewards through best-of-n and rejection-sampling fine-tuning, the RL method that cannot go far wrong, and say where it stops.
must_cover: Verifiable rewards: in domains where an output can be checked (a mathematics answer against the solution, code against tests, a fault tree or a safety-case argument against structural rules) the reward is exact and cheap, and satisfying it is the goal, to the extent that the verifier is complete. Section 9 shows what happens when it is not.

Best-of-n at inference: with per-sample success probability p, P(at least one of n passes) = 1 - (1 - p)^n. With a verifier this turns compute into accuracy; with a learned reward model it overoptimises (Section 5).

Best-of-n is itself a policy that has moved away from the base by a bounded amount: KL(pi_BoN || pi_ref) <= log n - (n - 1)/n (Stiennon et al. 2020; Gao et al. 2023; exact when no two samples tie, an upper bound in general, Beirami et al. 2024).

Rejection-sampling fine-tuning, also called expert iteration, RAFT, ReST, STaR or best-of-n distillation: sample N outputs per prompt from the current model, keep those the verifier accepts (and, if there is a judge, the best-judged of those), fine-tune on the kept set, repeat. The same idea with different filters and schedules (Anthony et al. 2017 for the name; Zelikman et al. 2022; Dong et al. 2023; Gulcehre et al. 2023).

It is an ordinary SFT loop with a data generator in front; it cannot go far wrong and often gets most of the way. Llama 2-Chat used rejection sampling before PPO; DeepSeek-R1 used a rejection-sampling SFT stage between its RL stages.

Its weaknesses: it learns only from successes (failures carry information that GRPO uses); prompts never solved contribute nothing, so the set drifts toward easy prompts (cap the kept samples per prompt); repeated rounds sharpen the policy onto its own successes and reduce diversity; the verifier's blind spots are learned along with its checks.
worked_examples: Coverage: p = 0.2 gives 1 - 0.8^8 = 0.832 at n = 8 and 0.972 at n = 16; p = 0.05 needs n = 45 to reach 0.90.

Yield and balance: 1,000 prompts, p = 0.3, n = 8 -> 2,400 accepted samples expected, but only 1000 x (1 - 0.7^8) = 942 prompts have at least one; keeping every accepted sample gives easy prompts several copies, capping at one per prompt gives 942 balanced examples.

Lab 5 Part A on the toy sums task: accept rate 0.44 -> 0.95 -> 0.99 over three rounds of sample-8, verify, keep, fine-tune; after three rounds the KL from the reference is 0.82 nats: the policy has sharpened onto its own correct answers.

figures.description: Left: the loop prompts -> sample n per prompt -> verifier (tick or cross per sample) -> keep ticks, at most k per prompt -> SFT on kept set -> updated policy -> back to sampling, with a note on the arrow from unsolved prompts 'contributes nothing'. Right: 1 - (1 - p)^n against n from 1 to 64 (log x-axis) for p = 0.05, 0.2 and 0.5.

checks: Why can expert iteration stop improving on hard prompts? -> If none of the n samples passes, the prompt contributes no training example, so the model never learns from it.

Best-of-16 against a complete verifier versus against a learned reward model: which can overoptimise? -> The learned reward model; with a complete verifier a high score is the goal itself, although an incomplete verifier can be gamed too.

sections.title: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards: GRPO
sections.purpose: Derive GRPO from the policy gradient, show how its group baseline and KL term work, and show how to design rewards that survive optimisation.
must_cover: Why verifiable rewards: preference data is expensive and a learned reward is hackable; where outputs can be checked the reward is exact and free. This is the setting behind the reasoning models of 2024-2025, and the setting of the running case study, whose arguments can be checked by deterministic structural rules.

GRPO (Shao et al. 2024; DeepSeek-AI 2025): for each prompt sample a group of G outputs from the current policy, score each, and use the group as the baseline: A_i = (r_i - mean(r_1..r_G)) / std(r_1..r_G). No value network. Show that r_i minus the group mean equals (G - 1)/G times r_i minus the mean of the other G - 1 rewards, so the group baseline is the leave-one-out baseline up to a constant factor (RLOO, Ahmadian et al. 2024).

The objective, as in the source: J(theta) = E[ (1/G) sum_i (1/|y_i|) sum_t min(rho_{i,t} A_i, clip(rho_{i,t}, 1 - epsilon, 1 + epsilon) A_i) - beta D_KL(pi_theta || pi_ref) ], rho_{i,t} = pi_theta(y_{i,t} | x, y_{i,<t}) / pi_theta_old(y_{i,t} | x, y_{i,<t}). With one gradient step per batch (as DeepSeekMath did) rho = 1 at the update and the clip does nothing: GRPO is then REINFORCE with a group baseline and a KL penalty.

The KL term is estimated per token with k3 = pi_ref/pi_theta - log(pi_ref/pi_theta) - 1. Derive: with u = pi_ref/pi_theta, E_{pi_theta}[u] = 1, so E[k3] = E[-log u] = KL(pi_theta || pi_ref) (unbiased); and log u <= u - 1 makes every term non-negative (low variance, never negative, unlike k1 = log(pi_theta/pi_ref)). In GRPO the KL sits in the loss; in PPO-RLHF it sits in the reward.
The source's grpo_advantages code (a group with zero variance gets zero advantage) and the per-token loss written in a few lines.

Memory: the policy and a frozen reference (with LoRA, one base). Compute: usually dominated by generating G samples per prompt; with long prompts the training passes, which reprocess the prompt for each of the G samples, can cost as much (the case study, Section 14). Hyperparameters that recur: G = 8 to 16 on modest budgets (DeepSeekMath used 64), epsilon = 0.2, beta = 0.04 (some later recipes drop the KL entirely, e.g. DAPO), learning rate 1e-6 for full weights.

Zero-variance groups: if every sample in a group gets the same reward (all right or all wrong) the group contributes no gradient. With binary rewards and pass rate p, the probability that a group carries signal is 1 - p^G - (1 - p)^G; prompts of the right difficulty are the ones that teach; filter or re-sample groups without signal (dynamic sampling, Yu et al. 2025).

Known biases of the original normalisation (Liu et al. 2025): dividing by |y_i| makes a long wrong answer's sequence log-probability fall more slowly than a short one's, so failures drift longer; dividing by the group std up-weights prompts that are nearly always or nearly never solved. Fixes: a constant normaliser and no std (Dr. GRPO), or token-level averaging over the whole group (DAPO).

Rewards in practice: a binary correctness reward plus a small format reward was enough for R1. A reward that can be satisfied trivially will be: a parseable empty artifact must score below a full one; partial credit per rule gives gradient before full correctness; cap judged terms rather than summing them freely; length drifts upward when longer outputs are more likely to contain a correct answer, so watch it and bound it if it does not carry quality. The case study's reward (Section 14) is built on these rules.

What R1 showed: RL from the base model with only rule-based accuracy and format rewards (R1-Zero) raised AIME 2024 pass@1 from 15.6% to 71.0% during training and produced long, self-checking chains of thought that nobody demonstrated: the clearest evidence that the objective, not the data, was teaching the behaviour. R1-Zero's outputs were hard to read and mixed languages; the released R1 added a small cold-start SFT stage, reasoning RL, a rejection-sampling SFT stage over a broad prompt set (about 800k samples) and a final RL stage for general preferences. Plain SFT of smaller Qwen and Llama bases on R1's outputs reached most of its quality and beat RL run directly on the small models.
Why GRPO rather than sample-verify-keep: it also learns from the failures in each group (negative advantages), and its signal is relative to the prompt's difficulty.

Length bias: two wrong answers in a group both have A = -0.6, lengths 200 and 800 tokens; the push on their sequence log-probabilities is A / |y| = -0.003 and -0.00075: the long wrong answer is penalised four times less.

sections.title: Safety, refusal and honesty
sections.purpose: Treat refusal, abstention and honesty as trainable behaviours with their own failure modes, measurements and reward design.
must_cover: Refusals are behaviours like any other: demonstrated in SFT, preferred in pairs, rewarded in RL. A refusal demonstration states briefly what cannot be done and offers a safe alternative. Helpfulness and harmlessness pull against each other (Bai et al. 2022a).

Constitutional AI (Bai et al. 2022b): a supervised phase in which the model critiques and revises its own outputs against written principles and is trained on the revisions, and an RL phase in which a model compares outputs against the principles to produce preferences (RL from AI feedback), replacing much of the human labelling.

Over-refusal: declining benign requests that pattern-match harmful ones ('How do I kill a Python process?'). Measured with a suite of benign-borderline prompts (XSTest: 250 safe prompts that resemble unsafe ones) exactly as harmful requests are measured with red-team prompts; the two rates are reported together, because either alone is maximised by a trivial policy.

Red-teaming: manual, by domain experts, and automated, with a language model generating attacks (Perez et al. 2022); findings become evaluation suites and training data; static suites saturate and must be refreshed.

Calibration after post-training, with expected calibration error recalled in one line from Module 01, Section 7 (as in Section 5), not re-defined: base models are often well calibrated on multiple-choice questions when confidence is read from the answer-token probabilities (Kadavath et al. 2022); the GPT-4 technical report shows post-training made its model's calibration markedly worse. A plausible mechanism in the training signal: comparisons reward answers that sound confident and complete, and a grader that scores abstention like an error rewards guessing. Measure calibration before and after each stage.

Abstention as a trained behaviour, with the threshold recalled in one line from Module 07, Section 10, not re-derived: with +1 for a correct answer, 0 for abstaining and -lambda for a wrong one, answering pays only when p > lambda / (1 + lambda), and 0/1 grading means always guess. What post-training adds: an RL reward or an evaluation that scores abstention like an error trains confident guessing (Kalai et al. 2025), so the reward must pay more for 'I do not know' than for a wrong answer; and the rule acts on the model's own estimate of p, so it is only as good as the model's calibration.

Honesty about actions: not claiming to have done what was not done. A model that says it has finished when it has not can be caught by a check on the artifact and penalised in training, not only blocked at runtime.

Sycophancy is the side-effect of rewarding agreement: preference data from people who like being agreed with produces it, and both humans and preference models sometimes prefer convincing sycophantic answers to correct ones (Sharma et al. 2024). Include pairs where the honest answer contradicts the user's premise.

A method for any deployed assistant: each documented failure family (claiming a task is complete when it is not, verdicts without evidence, a low-quality output saved over a good one, over-refusal, sycophantic agreement) defines a suite of prompts, a target behaviour and a reward term.

Lab 6's evidence from a 135M instruct model: asked for a bearing temperature it cannot know, it invents one ('a 100-degree Fahrenheit (40-degree Celsius) temperature', with a wrong conversion), and it does not refuse a request to bypass a press's safety interlock. In small models post-training covered format far more than safety or honesty.
worked_examples: A trade-off read with error bars (hypothetical numbers): a safety update moves refusal of harmful prompts from 97% to 99% (n = 200, standard errors 1.2 and 0.7 points) and refusal of benign-borderline prompts from 18% to 36% (n = 250, standard errors 2.4 and 3.0 points). The 2-point safety gain is within noise (a paired test on the same prompts agrees: a net gain of 4 refusals gives an exact McNemar p of at least 0.125, Section 12); the 18-point over-refusal increase is not.

One failure family turned into a suite, a target and a reward term (case study): citing evidence that is not in the brief. Suite: briefs whose evidence register lacks the item a claim needs. Target: the argument marks the claim unsupported and names the missing evidence. Reward: the checker's no-dangling-reference rule fails any citation of an evidence ID that is not in the register, so a fabricated citation loses rule credit and can never reach the judged term (Section 14's reward).

The off-diagonal error cells are labelled 'unsafe compliance (measured by red-team suite)' and 'over-refusal (measured by benign-borderline suite)'. Below, a trade-off curve: x-axis refusal rate on benign-borderline prompts, y-axis refusal rate on harmful prompts, traced as a safety knob moves, with the hypothetical before/after points (18%, 97%) and (36%, 99%).

Why report a refusal suite together with a benign-borderline suite? -> Each alone is maximised by a trivial policy: refuse everything, or comply with everything.

sections.title: Tools and agents
sections.purpose: Say what training for tool use adds to SFT and RL, and hand over to the AI Agents series for building agents.
must_cover: A model that calls tools has been trained on conversations containing tool calls in a fixed format (a JSON object naming the function and its arguments, inside model-specific markers rendered by the chat template), tool results as their own turn, and assistant turns that use them. Formats differ between model families.
Loss masking extends to tools: tool results are produced by the environment, like user turns, and are masked; training on them teaches the model to invent tool outputs.

Data: demonstrations (human or distilled trajectories) filtered by execution (sample, verify, keep: keep trajectories whose calls execute and whose final answer checks); Toolformer's self-supervised filter kept a candidate API call only if its result made the following text more likely (Schick et al. 2023); RL where the reward depends on the tool's result.

The behaviours that matter in an agent loop and need the most examples, because they are rare in naturally occurring data: deciding not to call a tool, reading a tool's error and changing course, and stopping.
Robustness of arguments (types, required fields) is trained and also enforced at serving by constrained decoding (Module 10).

An agent loop runs the model in exactly this mode; runtime guards (refusing to save an artifact that fails its checks, verifying a claimed completion before accepting it) are the runtime side of what this section trains for. The AI Agents series covers the agent loop, tool use, MCP, guardrails and agent evaluation.
worked_examples: Token accounting for one trajectory: system prompt 300 tokens, tool schemas 450, user 40, assistant tool call 35, tool result 600, assistant final answer 120: 1,545 tokens, of which 155 (10%) are trained.

An illustrative trajectory with generic markers (not any model's actual format), from the case study: the assistant emits {"name": "get_hazard", "arguments": {"id": "H-12"}}; the tool turn returns the hazard-log entry {"id": "H-12", "hazard": "relief valve fails to open on vessel overpressure", "severity": "catastrophic", "status": "open"}; the final assistant turn cites H-12 in the argument it drafts, and only the two assistant turns carry loss.

sections.title: Evaluation
sections.purpose: Say what replaces the loss after post-training, how each kind of evaluation fails, and how to tell a real difference from noise.
must_cover: The pretraining loss no longer means much after post-training: preference optimisation and RL optimise behaviour, and DPO can lower the likelihood of good answers (Section 7).

Instruction-following suites with verifiable constraints (IFEval: about 500 prompts with 25 kinds of checkable instruction, such as 'answer in exactly three bullet points'), and the domain's own checkers (for the case study, parse rate and structural pass rate).
A general-capability battery run before and after, to price the forgetting.

Behavioural suites built from the failure modes you have seen, pass or fail per case with programmatic checkers; checkers measure what they test, not what you meant (Lab 6: a base model that emits junk passes 'does not refuse').

Judged comparisons: a strong model compares two responses (MT-Bench: 80 multi-turn questions; its GPT-4 judge agreed with human preferences over 80% of the time, about as often as humans agree with each other; Chatbot Arena aggregates human votes with a Bradley-Terry model). Biases: position, length, self-preference, weak grading of mathematics. Mitigations: swap the positions and average, length-controlled win rates (Dubois et al. 2024), reference-guided grading, and a reported agreement rate with a human-labelled sample.

Contamination control: exact content hashes and n-gram overlap (the GPT-3 paper used 13-grams) between every training set, distillation prompts included, and every evaluation set; report how many examples were dropped; paraphrased contamination escapes n-gram checks.

An evaluation score is an estimate. Recall in one paragraph with a link to Module 01, Section 10, rather than re-deriving: the standard error of a pass rate sqrt(p(1 - p)/n) and its 95% interval of about +/-1.96 standard errors; the percentile bootstrap; paired comparisons on the same items (per-item differences, the paired bootstrap, McNemar's test on the discordant items). What post-training evaluation adds: suites are small (tens to hundreds of items), so the paired analysis is the default; when the information sits in a handful of discordant items the bootstrap's percentiles are unreliable, so use McNemar's exact form (under no difference each discordant item is a fair coin: twice the binomial tail); items generated from one template are not independent (resample templates, a cluster bootstrap); at temperature above zero, sample several times per item (Miller 2024).

Promotion gates: a candidate is promoted only if its domain metrics beat the incumbent beyond the interval and the general battery has not fallen beyond a stated tolerance; the artifact that ships (merged and quantised weights) is evaluated again.
worked_examples: A paired comparison on 50 items: A passes 36 (72%), B 31 (62%); both pass 28, only A 8, only B 3, both fail 11. Difference 10 points; paired normal interval [-2.7, 22.7]; paired bootstrap [-2, 24]; the unpaired half-width would be 18.3 points against 12.7 paired; McNemar's exact test on 8 versus 3 discordant items gives p = 0.227. The same rates on 500 items give [6.0, 14.0]: the same gap is noise on 50 items and a result on 500.

Position bias: 100 pairs judged in both orders; A wins 62 times when shown first and 44 when shown second; consistent verdicts 70 (A 38, B 32); swap-averaged win rate 53%; the 24 versus 6 split of inconsistent verdicts is the position bias.

Lab 6 (40-item suite, SmolLM2-135M base versus instruct): base 25% [12.5, 40], all of it from the benign category; instruct 37.5% [22.5, 52.5]; paired difference +12.5 points [2.5, 22.5] from 5 discordant items, all favouring the instruct model; McNemar's exact p = 0.0625. The bootstrap interval excludes zero and the exact test does not reject at 5%: 40 items cannot settle it.

Lab 6's simulated judge (400 pairs, equal true quality, model A 80 words longer on average, position bias 0.5 logits, length bias 0.4 logits per 100 words): A wins 65% when shown first and 47% when second; swap-averaging gives 56%, still 7 points above the true 49%; a length-controlled estimate (logistic regression on the length difference, read at zero) gives 49%.

What do you need before believing it? -> A paired analysis on the same items (discordant counts, paired interval or exact test), a check for clustering and for contamination; at 70% the unpaired standard error alone is about 4.6 points for the difference.
Why swap the positions in a pairwise judge? -> Position bias pushes every verdict the same way in one order; averaging both orders cancels it. It does not cancel length bias.

sections.title: Merging and averaging
sections.purpose: Explain when averaging weights works, the main merge methods, and how to merge adapters correctly.
must_cover: Two fine-tuned copies of the same base can be averaged weight by weight, and the average is often better than either (model soups, Wortsman et al. 2022). It works because fine-tunes of one base stay in a connected low-loss region (linear mode connectivity; Frankle et al. 2020); two networks trained from different initialisations do not, and averaging them destroys both.
Uniform soup versus greedy soup (add a model to the average only if held-out accuracy improves); averaging checkpoints along one run for a small free gain.
Task arithmetic (Ilharco et al. 2023): the task vector tau = theta_finetuned - theta_base; adding task vectors (with a scale lambda) combines skills; subtracting one removes a behaviour.

TIES-merging (Yadav et al. 2023): trim each task vector to its largest-magnitude entries, elect a sign per parameter from the sum of the trimmed values, and average only the entries that agree with it; DARE (Yu et al. 2024) randomly drops most delta entries and rescales the rest before merging.
Adapters: the update is the product B A, so merge the products (or concatenate the factors into a higher-rank adapter), never the averaged factors; the sum of two rank-r updates can have rank 2r.
None of it is guaranteed, all of it is cheap to try, and every merged candidate is evaluated like any other (Section 12).
worked_examples: TIES on five parameters with three task vectors tau1 = (0.50, -0.20, 0.02, 0.30, -0.40), tau2 = (0.40, 0.30, -0.01, -0.35, -0.05), tau3 = (-0.10, 0.25, 0.03, 0.20, -0.30). Plain mean: (0.267, 0.117, 0.013, 0.050, -0.250). Keep the 3 largest-magnitude entries of each vector: (0.5, 0, 0, 0.3, -0.4), (0.4, 0.3, 0, -0.35, 0), (0, 0.25, 0, 0.2, -0.3); elected signs (+, +, 0, +, -); disjoint mean (0.45, 0.275, 0, 0.25, -0.35). The fourth parameter keeps its majority direction (0.25) instead of cancelling to 0.05.

Adapter merging: B1 = (1, 0)^T, A1 = (1, 0) and B2 = (0, 1)^T, A2 = (0, 1). The average of the products is 0.5 I; the product of the averaged factors is a matrix with every entry 0.25, a different update of rank 1.

sections.title: The case study: a post-training recipe for a safety-case assistant
sections.purpose: Walk through a hypothetical post-training design for the running case study, with the reasoning and the arithmetic behind each choice.
must_cover: Framing: a hypothetical worked case, not anyone's plan or product. The model drafts and checks safety-case arguments for the pressure-relief system of a reactor vessel (claims, strategies, evidence, context) in a fixed JSON schema; a deterministic checker tests the structure (every claim supported, every leaf cites evidence, no dangling references, no cycles, every hazard-log entry in the brief addressed). Requests follow the workload shared by Modules 07-10: about 4,000 tokens in (a 3,000-token stable prefix of system prompt, schema and fixed reference text, plus about 1,000 tokens of hazard-log entries and the engineer's request) and up to 2,000 tokens out.

Step 0, baselines: the instruct release, prompted with the deployment's system prompt, on the golden set (parse rate, checker pass rate, judge coverage): the bar every later stage must clear, because prompting it is the cheap alternative to all of this; the instruct release and the starting checkpoint on the general battery. Module 08's domain baselines (domain perplexity and a small domain test set) already decided whether continued pretraining was needed.

Step 1, the starting point, with its rule: if Module 08's baselines showed that continued pretraining was needed, SFT starts from the CPT checkpoint, which is a base model with no chat behaviour, so the SFT mix must carry general instruction data (conversation, refusals, tool calls) as well as the domain's, and the chat-template tokens must be checked and, if untrained, initialised and trained (Section 3; plain domain text never contains them, so continued pretraining does not teach them); otherwise SFT starts from the instruct release, whose template tokens are trained and whose general behaviours come for free, and only the domain's are added. This case study takes the first path: Module 08 chose and costed continued pretraining for it (1.8B domain tokens plus 0.2B tokens of replay), and the checkpoint is assumed to have passed that module's go/no-go rule. Either way the licence must permit fine-tuning and the planned distillation.

Step 2, SFT with LoRA from the CPT checkpoint: r = 64, alpha = 128, all linear layers, plus the template tokens' rows of the input embedding and the output head made trainable (a few rows of 4,096 values, initialised as in Section 3); learning rate 1e-4, cosine with 3% warmup, 2 epochs, packed 8,192-token rows, the deployment's system prompts verbatim, English and Chinese briefs in their deployed proportions. Data, about 50M tokens: checker-verified example arguments distilled from a stronger model, scripted edit pairs ('change only what was asked'), refusal and abstention examples (evidence missing -> say so), and general instruction data, about a third of the tokens to start with: a larger share than an instruct start would need, because the CPT checkpoint has none of this behaviour; the share is raised if the general battery falls. Gate: parse rate and checker pass rate beat the prompted instruct release by more than their intervals; the general battery within a stated tolerance of the instruct release's.

Step 3, RL with verifiable rewards (GRPO) rather than DPO, because a deterministic checker gives exact rewards on the model's own samples, while DPO would need pairs, which risk likelihood displacement when they are off-policy. G = 8; beta = 0.04 KL to the SFT model; about 3,000 prompts drawn like real requests, for 2 epochs, one gradient step per batch; the full golden set after each epoch.

The reward function, generalised from the source: parse_argument(reply) is None -> 0.0 (nothing below is reachable for prose); 0.5 x rules passed / rules total; +0.2 x preserved fraction for edit briefs; +0.3 x min(judge coverage, 1.0) only when every rule passes; -0.2 if degenerate (every hazard given the same risk rating, or every claim citing the same evidence item). Each term's reason: partial credit gives gradient before full correctness; the judge sees only rule-clean artifacts, which bounds its cost and stops its preferences rewarding broken structure; min caps the judged term; the penalty blocks the shortcuts the rules cannot see; a parseable empty artifact scores below a full one.

Step 4: merge the adapter into bf16 weights, quantise for serving (Module 10 serves this merged, quantised artifact, about 5.5 GB at 4 bits), evaluate the quantised artifact again on the golden set and the general battery, record its hash, promote.

Risks and monitors: length drift (track mean length every evaluation); reward hacking (a human reads a sample of high-reward outputs each epoch); forgetting (general battery); over-refusal on benign briefs; contamination between distillation prompts and the golden set (hash check).
The alternative path: DPO on on-policy pairs ranked by the judge, for behaviours no checker can score (for example the clarity of the argument's prose).
worked_examples: SFT compute (Section 4's arithmetic under Module 06's convention): 1e8 token-passes (50M tokens, 2 epochs) x 4.30e10 FLOPs = 4.30e18 FLOPs: 3.0 GPU-hours at the assumed 4e14 FLOP/s per H100.

GRPO budget: P = 3,000 prompts x G = 8 x E = 2 epochs = 48,000 samples of up to 2,000 tokens: 96M generated tokens. At an assumed 2,500 generated tokens per second per H100 (bf16 policy, continuous batching; an assumption to replace with a measurement, of the order Module 10, Section 11 derives for this workload), generation takes 10.7 GPU-hours. The 4,000-token prompts are prefilled once per group, the prefix shared by its eight samples: 6,000 x 7.61e13 FLOPs = 4.6e17, 0.3 GPU-hours. The training passes run over whole 6,000-token sequences, prompt included: the LoRA policy's forward and activation-gradient passes plus the reference's forward cost 6 N_matmul + 8LTd = 6.06e10 FLOPs per token at T = 6,000, and 288M token-passes give 1.75e19 FLOPs, 12.1 GPU-hours. About 23 GPU-hours per run before the judge's cost: with long shared prompts the training passes cost as much as generation.

Cost at Module 07's assumed USD 2.50 per H100-hour (an assumption, as of 2026; write 'USD', never a dollar sign): SFT about USD 7.50, one GRPO run about USD 58 plus the judge's calls; three runs of each come to about USD 200, the sense in which post-training is cheap (Section 1).

Reward walk-through for four replies to briefs with 12 rules: (a) prose with no artifact -> 0.0; (b) a parseable artifact passing 9 of 12 rules -> 0.5 x 9/12 = 0.375; (c) a rule-clean edit preserving 90% of the prior content with judge coverage 0.8 -> 0.5 + 0.18 + 0.24 = 0.92; (d) a rule-clean new artifact in which every claim cites the same evidence item, coverage 0.6 -> 0.5 + 0.18 - 0.2 = 0.48.

figures.description: The case-study pipeline: Module 08's CPT checkpoint (with a dashed alternative entry 'instruct release, if CPT was not needed') -> baselines (prompted instruct release on the golden set; general battery) -> SFT with LoRA and trainable template-token rows (data mix listed: verified distillations, edit pairs, refusal and abstention examples, general instruction data about a third) -> gate 1 (parse rate, checker pass rate, general battery against the instruct release) -> GRPO with the reward assembled from checker, preservation check, judge (only for rule-clean outputs) and degeneracy penalty -> gate 2 (golden set, length, human sample) -> merge -> quantise (about 5.5 GB at 4 bits) -> re-evaluate -> hash -> promote. Compute annotated under each training box (about 3 GPU-hours; about 23 GPU-hours).

checks: Why does the judge's term apply only to rule-clean artifacts? -> It bounds the judge's cost, keeps the judge's preferences from rewarding structurally broken outputs, and puts the verifiable rules first.
Why GRPO and not DPO for the main stage? -> A deterministic checker gives exact rewards on the model's own samples; DPO would need pairs, and off-policy pairs risk likelihood displacement.

Why does starting from the CPT checkpoint rather than the instruct release change the SFT recipe? -> The CPT checkpoint is a base model: turn-taking, refusals and the tool format must be taught again, so general instruction data takes a larger share of the mix, and the chat-template tokens may be untrained and need their rows initialised and made trainable.
